title: Shrink the Squared Gaps
statement:
You get two integer arrays a and b of the same length n, and two budgets k1 and k2. The score is the sum of (a[i] − b[i])² over all i.

A move adds 1 to or subtracts 1 from one element. You may make at most k1 moves on elements of a and at most k2 moves on elements of b. Values may go negative.

Return the smallest score you can reach.

examples.why: The gaps are 3, 0 and 5, and you have 3 moves in total. Spend two on the 5 (now 3), and one on either 3: 2² + 0² + 3² = 13. Spreading moves evenly from the start would be worse.
The gaps total 5, so 5 of the 10 moves close them all. The rest can go unused.
Moving a down and moving b up both shrink the same gap, so the budgets simply add up: 10 − 6 = 4.

hints: Does it matter whether a move is spent on a[i] or on b[i]?
Only the gaps d[i] = |a[i] − b[i]| matter, and you have k = k1 + k2 moves that each shrink one gap by 1. Which gap should a single move go to?

Always shrinking the largest gap is optimal, because squaring punishes big gaps most. Do it in bulk: binary-search the level T such that cutting every gap down to T fits the budget, then spend the leftover moves lowering some of the gaps that sit at T by one more.

explain.intuition:
Moving a[i] towards b[i] and moving b[i] towards a[i] do the same thing, so pool the budgets: k = k1 + k2 moves, each shrinking one gap d[i] = |a[i] − b[i]| by 1. Shrinking a gap from d to d − 1 saves 2d − 1, which is largest for the largest gap. So each move should hit the current largest gap.

One move at a time is too slow for k up to 2·10⁹. Repeatedly cutting the tallest gap is the same as lowering a water level T over the gaps: every gap above T is cut down to T. Binary-search the lowest T the budget can pay for. Whatever is left over is smaller than the number of gaps now sitting at T, so those extra moves lower that many gaps to T − 1. If the budget covers the sum of all gaps, the answer is 0.
steps: Compute d[i] = |a[i] − b[i]| and k = k1 + k2. If sum(d) ≤ k, return 0.
Binary-search the smallest T in [0, max d] with Σ max(0, d[i] − T) ≤ k.
Cut every gap above T down to T and subtract the cost from k.
The leftover k is less than the number of gaps equal to T; lower k of them to T − 1.
Return the sum of squares of the final gaps.
pitfalls: Spending moves evenly or on the first gaps. Squares reward cutting the biggest gap: in example 1, two moves on the 5 beat one each on the 3 and the 5.
Forgetting the leftover moves after reaching level T; the binary search alone leaves some budget unused.
Overflowing 32-bit integers: the score can reach 10⁵ · (10⁵)² = 10¹⁵, and k1 + k2 can exceed 2³¹.

solutions.title: One move at a time on the largest gap
solutions.idea: Pool the budgets, cap them at the total gap, and repeatedly find the largest gap and shrink it by 1.

solutions.title: Binary search the water level
solutions.idea: Find the lowest level T the budget can cut every gap down to, then use the leftover moves on gaps sitting at T.

followups: Gap values are small (at most 10⁵). How can a count per gap value replace the binary search?
Each move on a[i] has its own price. Does the greedy still work?
